title: Cyclospora Outbreak Surges Past 6,700 Cases Across 34 US States as CDC Ramps Up Tracking
excerpt: The parasitic illness, linked to contaminated lettuce at Taco Bell locations, has caused 141 hospitalisations with no deaths reported.
body:
• More than 6,700 confirmed or probable cases of cyclosporiasis have been reported across 34 US states since May, with 141 hospitalisations and no deaths.
  • The FDA traced the largest cluster to shredded iceberg lettuce from a Mexican supplier used by Taco Bell in five states, though it later declared a positive lab test a false positive.
  • The CDC is publishing surveillance updates more frequently than in previous years due to the unusual surge — case counts are roughly 6.5 times higher than the typical 250 reported by this point in the season.
  • Health officials warn that symptoms can persist for weeks if untreated and recommend thorough washing of fresh produce.

An Outbreak Far Beyond the Seasonal Norm

A parasitic illness causing severe gastrointestinal symptoms has spread across 34 US states at a pace that has alarmed federal health officials. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed 1,644 laboratory-verified cases of cyclosporiasis as of July 13, with an additional 5,100 probable cases under investigation — bringing the total to more than 6,700.

The numbers are strikingly unusual. By this point in a typical year, the CDC has received roughly 250 reports. The 2026 season is running at more than six times the normal rate, prompting the agency to increase the frequency of its surveillance updates beyond what it has done in previous years.

At least 141 people have been hospitalised. No deaths have been reported.

The Taco Bell Connection — And a False Positive

The FDA's investigation zeroed in on the largest outbreak cluster: 1,644 cases linked to Taco Bell locations across Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, and West Virginia. Ingredient-level analysis of 190 cases found that 90 percent of those interviewed had consumed shredded iceberg lettuce. The FDA's traceback investigation identified a single supplier of iceberg lettuce from Guanajuato, Mexico, used by the affected Taco Bell locations.

Taco Bell has committed to stopping all purchases from the identified supplier, and Taylor Fresh Foods voluntarily removed all its iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the US market.

In a twist, the FDA announced on July 19 that a laboratory test result initially showing cyclospora contamination in Taylor Farms lettuce was actually a false positive. The agency confirmed there are no verified positive samples as of that date — though the epidemiological link between the outbreak and the lettuce remains under investigation.

What Is Cyclosporiasis?

Cyclosporiasis is caused by Cyclospora cayetanensis, a microscopic parasite that infects the small intestine. Unlike bacterial food-borne pathogens like salmonella and E. coli, cyclospora only infects humans and cannot spread through meat. It is transmitted through food or water contaminated with human faecal matter containing the parasite's oocysts.

Symptoms include watery diarrhoea — often described by doctors as "explosive" — stomach cramps, nausea, loss of appetite, fatigue, and weight loss. Unlike many stomach illnesses that resolve in days, cyclosporiasis can persist for weeks or even months without treatment. Antibiotics are effective against the infection.

"It can't be spread through meat. It's a parasite spread through produce infected with human fecal matter."

— Dr. Ewen Todd, food-safety consultant and adjunct professor, Michigan State University

How to Protect Yourself

Health officials recommend cooking fruits and vegetables when possible, as heating food to at least 158°F (70°C) kills the parasite. For raw produce like salad greens, thorough washing for at least one minute is advised, though experts note that washing may not remove all cyclospora spores.

The CDC has flagged several produce categories previously associated with outbreaks: raspberries, basil, salad mixes, cilantro, berry mixes, lettuce, and snow peas. People with weakened immune systems or older adults may want to exercise extra caution with these items during the summer outbreak season, which typically runs from May through August.

Anyone experiencing diarrhoea lasting longer than 48 hours should contact a healthcare provider for testing. The CDC expects case counts to continue climbing due to an approximately six-week lag between illness onset and case reporting.
